failure_modes.description: The assumption that riblet dimensions (50-200μm height, 100-400μm spacing) are optimized for Re 500,000 is completely unsubstantiated. No scaling laws or computational fluid dynamics evidence provided to support this specific dimension range.
failure_modes.evidence: Riblet effectiveness is highly Reynolds number dependent, and the proposed dimensions may be completely inappropriate for the target flow conditions.

failure_modes.description: The claim that riblets lift streamwise vortices away from the surface directly contradicts established literature showing riblets work primarily by inhibiting cross-stream vortex motion, not by lifting vortices away from the wall.
failure_modes.evidence: Multiple peer-reviewed studies (Bechert et al., 1997; Walsh, 1980) demonstrate riblets reduce drag by creating longitudinal grooves that trap vortices, not by lifting them away.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis ignores the fundamental difference between external flow (shark skin) and internal flow (pipe flow) boundary conditions. In pipe flow, the boundary layer development is fundamentally different and riblet performance cannot be directly extrapolated.
failure_modes.evidence: Pipe flow has different boundary layer characteristics, including developing vs. fully developed regions, that don't exist in external flows where shark skin riblets have been tested.

failure_modes.description: Numerous studies have already tested riblets in pipe applications with mixed results, often showing no significant drag reduction or even increased drag depending on manufacturing quality and flow conditions.
failure_modes.evidence: Studies by Bacher & Koury (1991) and others have shown riblets in pipes often perform worse than expected due to manufacturing imperfections and flow alignment issues.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis predicts a specific 6-9% drag reduction, but existing data suggests riblets typically achieve maximum drag reduction of 5-10% under ideal conditions, making this claim overly optimistic and easily falsifiable.
failure_modes.evidence: The claimed 6-9% reduction is at the upper end of the theoretical maximum for riblets, which rarely exceed 5-10% even in ideal laboratory conditions.

failure_modes.description: The hypothesis completely ignores practical implementation challenges in real pipe systems, including cleaning, maintenance, and long-term durability of micro-structured surfaces in harsh environments.
failure_modes.evidence: Industrial pipes face erosion, corrosion, and cleaning operations that would quickly degrade or destroy delicate micro-riblet structures.
